claims.text: Rapid heating and cooling impose kinetic constraints during noble-metal HEA nanoparticle synthesis.
These kinetic constraints prevent adequate atomic diffusion and intermixing.
Insufficient diffusion and intermixing cause elemental segregation and phase separation.
Insufficient diffusion and intermixing contribute to uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Conventional rapid thermal processing of the stated precursors typically yields non-equilibrium multiphase products.
The controlled intervention is gradual heating with intermediate isothermal holds and controlled cooling, without changing elemental composition.
The proposed heating rate is approximately 3–5 °C/min under an inert atmosphere.
Intermediate-temperature holds enhance atomic rearrangement and intermixing.
Rapid thermal processing immobilizes the precursors and prevents sufficient atomic diffusion for uniform phase formation.
Intermediate holds minimize elemental segregation by providing time for atomic rearrangement.
Configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase FCC structure after sufficient atomic intermixing.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, the controlled profile will produce a more uniform single-phase FCC product.
The controlled profile will reduce elemental segregation relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
The controlled profile will produce a more homogeneous particle-size distribution and morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Excessive thermal exposure can cause grain growth or precursor decomposition.
Failure of intermediate holds to produce a statistically significant improvement in FCC phase uniformity and segregation relative to the no-hold control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
